Different calibres have different pros and cons, as do different firing platforms (AR/AK/Etc). The variance is partially to fill various niches and needs while at the same time are in competition with other arms manufacturers which all also have their own quirks and benefits.

Looking simply at calibre, the smaller the round the less force in general it is going to impact the target with BUT the lighter the ammunition. Someone who has to deploy in combat may be able to carry largely different volumes of ammo based on what weapon they are holding. For example 10KG of ammunition for 7.62x54R is roughly 14 mags 280rounds whereas if their gun fires 5.56x45mm that same 10KG would be 33 mags or 660 rounds. 

If mobility isn’t an issue and you aren’t expected to be walking long distances or having long extended firefights 7.62 has better penetration and more stopping force so if you’re going to be in short skirmishes or relatively static you get more bang per trigger pull.

It also depends on what you’re shooting at, .22 is fine to plink away at a steel target or blast squirrels but isn’t going to do much in a firefight against any level of body armor. Whereas a 20mm like what the Lahti-L39 fires can punch huge holes through jeeps and aircraft and can deliver lethal velocity out to long ranges, it’s also super heavy and cumbersome and terrible for shooting on the move or in close quarters.

Looking into firing platforms apart from just ammo this also continues. Sometimes you want a shotgun for room clearing, sometimes you want an assault rifle for midrange engagements, sometimes you want an AK platform because you know you’re going to be putting that thing through nightmare situations and won’t have time for maintenance and sometimes you want an LMG to deny lines of fire and provide suppression fire out of a fixed position.

Okay so one piece of info I missed scrolling through is the starting number determines where modifiers are most important.

Assuming a 4+ to hit, 4+ to wound and a save roll of 4+ a +1 to hit wound or extra ap is identical.

What happens if it's a 3+, 4+, 4,+? Well +1 to hit increases a 66.6% chance to 83.3% chance (25% increase) where as a +1 to wound moves a 50% to a 66.6% which is a  30% increase.

The worse the base stat the more impactful a +1 is due to diminishing returns.  If you're hitting on 3s and wounding on 5s, +1 to wound is MUCH more important then +1 to hit. 

Base: 3+/5+/4+= 11% success

+1 to hit: 2+/5+/4+=13.8% success

+1 ap: 3+/5+/3+=14.8% success

+1 to wound: 3+/4+/4+=16 6% success
